n0001.title: Replication crisis
n0001.gist: Many published findings across science fail to replicate because of flawed incentives and statistics, prompting reform efforts.
n0001.question: replication crisis — why do so many scientific findings fail to repeat, and how can science fix this? (causes and reforms surveyed)

n0002.title: Defining the Crisis
n0002.gist: The crisis means published results often fail to repeat; understanding it requires distinguishing replication from reproducibility and knowing how p-values and statistical power work.
n0002.question: replication crisis — what do reproducibility, replication and statistical significance actually mean? (definitions)

n0003.title: Authors and credits
n0003.gist: The Wikimedia contributors and reading time.

n0006.title: Introducing the Crisis
n0006.gist: Ioannidis's influential claim that most published findings are false frames the crisis, which arises because failed reproductions in psychology, medicine, and other sciences undermine confidence in results.

n0011.title: Defining Reproducibility and Replication
n0011.gist: Researchers distinguish reproducibility, which reanalyzes existing data, from replication, which repeats a study with new data, and separate direct, systematic, and conceptual replication types.

n0020.title: Statistical Hypothesis Testing Basics
n0020.gist: A hypothesis counts as supported when results are statistically significant, meaning unlikely under a 'null hypothesis' of no true effect, formalized through effect sizes and test statistics.

n0028.title: Significance, Power, and P-values
n0028.gist: A null-hypothesis test's accuracy depends on its significance level (the false-positive rate), its statistical power (the true-positive rate), and the p-value summarizing how extreme the data are.

n0042.title: Origins and Early Evidence
n0042.gist: A string of failed replications in the early 2010s, building on decades of earlier warnings, turned scattered doubts into a named crisis across psychology and medicine.
n0042.question: replication crisis's origins — what events and prior warnings turned isolated doubts into a recognized crisis? (precursors and earlier warnings)

n0043.title: Precursors to the Crisis
n0043.gist: Failed replications of a famous social-priming study, a parapsychology experiment, and low biomedical replication rates, plus evidence of widespread p-hacking, together triggered the crisis in the early 2010s.

n0049.title: Early Warnings and Historical Roots
n0049.gist: Concerns about weak replication, low statistical power, and biased reporting had been voiced since the 1950s-70s, long before the 2010s crisis gave the problem its name.

n0057.title: Psychology Replication Findings
n0057.gist: Large coordinated projects found that only about a third to half of psychology studies replicated successfully, with replicated effects often only half the original size.

n0063.title: Medicine and Cancer Biology Findings
n0063.gist: Reviews of medical and cancer studies found only about 11-44% replicated, with effect sizes shrinking sharply and surveyed researchers often unable to reproduce published results.

n0067.title: Other Disciplines
n0067.gist: Beyond psychology, poor replication rates also appear in nutrition science, economics, water-resource research, and research involving large language models, each for its own reasons.
n0067.question: replication crisis beyond psychology — which other fields show similar failures, and why? (several fields compared)

n0068.title: Nutrition and Economics Findings
n0068.gist: In nutrition science most food-cancer claims lack robust support, while economics replication attempts succeed only about 61% of the time, with effect sizes often inflated.

n0075.title: In water resource management
n0075.gist: A study of nearly 2,000 water-resource management articles estimated that only a tiny fraction, 0.6% to 6.8%, could even be reproduced given the information provided.

n0079.title: Research on and with large language models
n0079.gist: Fast-changing, closed commercial language models and unreported code, data, or prompts make both research on these models and research using them hard to reproduce, prompting new checklists.
n0079.sourceHeading: In research on and with large language models

n0086.title: Surveys of Researchers and Citation Patterns
n0086.gist: Large surveys show most scientists have failed to reproduce others' work, yet still trust the literature, while studies that fail to replicate tend to get cited more often.

n0091.title: Causes: Publication and Practice
n0091.gist: Science's drive to publish positive results, reporting gaps, mathematical slips, and flexible research choices together inflate false positives and make studies hard to redo.
n0091.question: causes of non-replication — how do publication pressures and everyday research practices combine to produce unreliable findings? (several structural causes)

n0092.title: Historical and Sociological Causes
n0092.gist: Rapid growth in publications, pressure to publish or perish, the commercialization of research, and science's shifting social role have been blamed for declining research quality over decades.

n0100.title: Publication Bias
n0100.gist: Journals favor positive, significant results, leaving negative findings in a 'file drawer,' which skews the literature and, combined with many false hypotheses, inflates false-positive findings.

n0107.title: Mathematical Errors
n0107.gist: Even top journals contain many simple statistical errors, such as mismatched p-values and tests that wrongly ask whether one effect differs from zero rather than from another.

n0112.title: "Publish or perish" culture
n0112.gist: Intense career pressure to publish pushes researchers toward results that look significant over results that are true, discouraging the time-consuming, less-rewarded work of replication.

n0119.title: Standards of Reporting
n0119.gist: Many papers omit details needed to redo a study, such as exact protocols or reagents, and biased interpretation of null versus positive results from instruments compounds the problem.

n0125.title: Questionable Research Practices
n0125.gist: Researchers often exploit flexible choices in design and analysis, such as selective reporting or HARKing, and in extreme cases outright fraud, both of which inflate false positives.

n0136.title: Low Statistical Power
n0136.gist: Psychology, neuroscience, and economics studies typically have far less than the recommended 80% statistical power, meaning even a true effect is unlikely to be confirmed on repeat.

n0145.title: Causes: Statistical and Contextual
n0145.gist: Weak statistical power, biased effect-size estimates, flawed meta-analysis methods, hidden context-dependence, and misunderstood probability theory all make replication less likely than it should be.
n0145.question: statistical causes — why do power, bias and context make replication fail even without misconduct? (several mechanisms)

n0146.title: Positive Effect Size Bias
n0146.gist: Underpowered studies that do replicate tend to report systematically smaller effects than the original, because small samples inflate whichever estimate happens to pass significance.

n0152.title: Problems of Meta-analysis
n0152.gist: Combining many studies' results runs into its own flaws, since a single bad study can skew a whole meta-analysis and fixes like the 'fail-safe number' are themselves imperfect.

n0160.title: Researcher Degrees of Freedom and P-hacking
n0160.gist: Many small, defensible choices in collecting and analyzing data create a 'garden of forking paths,' so flexible or early-stopped analyses can manufacture significance even with no real effect.

n0171.title: Statistical Heterogeneity
n0171.gist: Even exact replications often find true effect sizes vary widely across studies, a heterogeneity so large in psychology that similar results are unlikely even with huge samples.

n0178.title: Context Sensitivity
n0178.gist: Psychological effects may depend on hidden contextual factors, and reanalysis of major replication projects found that more context-sensitive effects were less likely to replicate successfully.

n0183.title: Bayesian Explanation
n0183.gist: Bayesian probability shows that rejecting the null hypothesis at 5% significance does not mean a 95% chance the alternative is true, especially when the hypothesis was unlikely beforehand.

n0191.title: Problem with Null Hypothesis Testing
n0191.gist: In 'soft' sciences where almost everything correlates somewhat, rejecting the null hypothesis barely supports any specific alternative, so many false hypotheses may simply be true beforehand.

n0204.title: Public Response and Credibility
n0204.gist: Failed replications drew public and academic attention, sparking defensive backlash in psychology and a broader push toward a more transparent 'credibility revolution.'
n0204.question: public response — how did scientists and the public react, and what change followed? (reaction then reform)

n0205.title: Public Awareness and Perceptions
n0205.gist: Surveys suggest most of the public has not heard of replication failures, and those who have mostly see replication efforts as a sign science polices its own quality.

n0209.title: Response in Academia
n0209.gist: A prominent psychologist's public attack on replication critics as 'bullying' drew sharp rebuttal from a statistician who pointed to her own flawed, uncorrected published statistics.

n0213.title: Credibility Revolution
n0213.gist: Some psychologists frame the crisis as grounds for a 'credibility revolution' emphasizing transparency, pre-registration, and stronger evidence standards, alongside calls to make clinical research patient-centered.

n0220.title: Reform in Scientific Publishing
n0220.gist: Journals and researchers now push pre-registration, blind review of methods before results, smaller significance thresholds, and clearer reporting to curb bias before publication.
n0220.question: reform in publishing — what concrete changes to journals and methods aim to prevent unreliable results from being published? (several proposed reforms)

n0221.title: Reform in Scientific Publishing
n0221.gist: Metascience, the study of how research itself is done, drives efforts such as pre-registration and new reporting guidelines meant to fix incentives and improve peer review.

n0226.title: Presentation of Methodology
n0226.gist: Poor reporting of experimental and statistical methods is seen as a major cause of non-replication, prompting calls for cultural change and stricter journal rules, though over-rigid rules worry some.

n0231.title: Result-blind Peer Review
n0231.gist: Over 140 psychology journals now accept studies based on their methods before results are known, and early evidence shows this yields far more null results than usual.

n0235.title: Pre-registration of Studies
n0235.gist: Registered reports require authors to submit their methods and analysis plan before collecting data, guaranteeing publication regardless of outcome to curb bias toward significant findings.

n0240.title: Metadata and Digital Tools for Tracking Replications
n0240.gist: Proposed digital tools and rating systems would let readers, reviewers, or journals easily track how often a study has been repeated and whether it held up.
n0240.sourceHeading: Metadata and digital tools for tracking replications

n0244.title: Requiring Smaller P-values
n0244.gist: A widely signed proposal to tighten the significance threshold from p<0.05 to p<0.005 aimed to cut false positives, but a rival group's objections left neither standard widely adopted.

n0249.title: Addressing Misinterpretation of P-values
n0249.gist: Even a very small p-value can still carry a surprisingly high false-positive risk if the tested hypothesis was unlikely beforehand, so some propose reporting that risk alongside p-values.

n0255.title: Encouraging Larger Sample Sizes
n0255.gist: Because small samples both exaggerate effect sizes and tempt researchers into overfitting models with too many variables, replication typically needs larger samples and techniques like cross-validation.

n0261.title: Replication Efforts
n0261.gist: Funders, universities and new databases now actively support and track replication studies themselves, treating them as valuable research rather than afterthoughts.
n0261.question: replication efforts — how are institutions now funding, teaching and tracking attempts to repeat past studies? (several initiatives)

n0262.title: Replication Efforts
n0262.gist: Foundations and governments have begun funding replication studies directly, including million-dollar grants that launched organizations devoted to studying and improving research practices.

n0267.title: Emphasis in Post-secondary Education
n0267.gist: Some universities now teach research methods through student-led replication attempts rather than original studies, and some recommend graduate students complete a replication before earning their degree.

n0271.title: Replication Database
n0271.gist: Growing concern about research waste from redundant replication attempts has led to new databases that track which studies have been repeated, including robot-assisted testing of cancer claims.

n0278.title: Involving Original Authors
n0278.gist: Replications succeed far more often when original authors are involved, since published methods are often too vague, which has spurred large international collaborations that pool resources and samples.

n0283.title: Broader Changes and Appendices
n0283.gist: Beyond fixing single studies, some argue science needs triangulation across methods, complex-systems thinking, and theory-revision, alongside open data and source lists.
n0283.question: broader change — should science move past simple replication toward triangulating methods and revising theories themselves? (three proposals, plus reference lists)

n0284.title: Emphasize triangulation, not just replication
n0284.gist: Two researchers argue that repeating the same method can entrench shared errors, so findings should instead be checked by independent methods whose different weaknesses make agreement more meaningful.

n0291.title: Complex Systems Paradigm
n0291.gist: Some argue psychology wrongly assumes mental variables are stable and independent, when a 'complex systems' view in which variables interact and shift with context may better explain failed replications.

n0297.title: Replication Should Seek to Revise Theories
n0297.gist: Replication alone cannot resolve the crisis unless failed or successful attempts are used to prune and rebuild stronger theories, aided by openly shared data, code, and software.
n0297.sourceHeading: Replication should seek to revise theories
